Efficiently Representing Algorithms with Chain-of-Thought Transformers

Yanhong Li Affiliation: Allen Institute for AI Email: yanhongl@allenai.org    Anej Svete Affiliation: ETH Zürich Email: asvete@ethz.ch    Ashish Sabharwal Affiliation: Allen Institute for AI Email: ashishs@allenai.org    William Merrill Affiliation: Allen Institute for AI Email: willm@allenai.org
Abstract

The increasing popularity of reasoning models—language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer—is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the Word RAM model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on 𝒪⁡(log⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}(\log n)-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms? For instance, can they sort nn items in 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}(n\log n) steps or run Dijkstra’s algorithm in 𝒪⁡(E+V​log⁡V){{\mathcal{O}}}(E+V\log V) steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: continuous CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a hybrid architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT can efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in nn. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a “flat” instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions—in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

1 Introduction

It has been known for a while that chain of thought (CoT) makes transformers Turing complete—able to simulate any algorithm in principle (Pérez et al., 2021). This justifies the empirical practice of training reasoning models to solve complex tasks (Snell et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026, e.g.,). However, the ability to simulate a Turing machine (TM) does not immediately translate to being able to implement interpretable algorithms efficiently: while TMs provide an established framework for analyzing computational complexity, they are not practical for designing real-world algorithms. For instance, sorting n{{n}} items takes only 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}\log{{n}})}} steps on a random-access machine (RAM)—an idealized computer whose memory cells can be read and written in unit time at arbitrary addresses, formalized in Section 2.1—because each comparison and swap touches an arbitrary array entry in a single step. A TM has no such random access: to reach the addressed cell it must move its head there, scanning a tape region of length up to 𝒪⁡(n+t){{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}+{{t}}) per access. Simulating these 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}\log{{n}})}} RAM steps on a TM therefore costs up to 𝒪⁡(n2​log⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}^{2}\log{{n}}) steps, and on a single-tape TM sorting provably requires Ω⁡(n2/log⁡n){{\Omega}}({{n}}^{2}/\log{{n}}) steps (Hennie, 1965). This overhead is not a quirk of the analysis—it reflects a fundamental mismatch between TMs and algorithms that rely on random memory access or word-level arithmetic. This paper asks: can CoT transformers efficiently simulate algorithms as written in textbooks? We answer affirmatively.

The natural model for describing textbook algorithms efficiently and concisely is the Word RAM. A Word RAM program stores data in a random-access memory (RAM) partitioned into words of w=Θ⁡(log⁡(n+t)){{w}}={{\Theta}}(\log({{n}}+{{t}})) bits—wide enough to address any of the 𝒪⁡(n+t){{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}+{{t}}) cells the program may touch during a t{{t}}-step execution—and it executes a program one instruction at a time, where each instruction runs in 𝒪⁡(1){{\mathcal{O}}}(1) steps. Its primitive operations—memory reads and writes, integer arithmetic, bitwise operations, and comparisons—correspond directly to the operations of modern programming languages and the algorithms textbooks describe. Thus, the standard complexity bounds practitioners know about correspond naturally to the algorithms expressed in the Word RAM model. For example, sorting takes 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}\log{{n}}) Word RAM steps and Dijkstra’s algorithm takes 𝒪⁡(E+V​log⁡V){{\mathcal{O}}}(E+V\log V).

Existing CoT expressivity results establish computational universality by simulating Turing machines (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). These constructions, however, operate entirely at the TM-instruction level: each CoT token encodes one tape symbol, and each decoding step simulates one TM transition. Routing a Word RAM program of t{{t}} steps through this construction therefore costs 𝒪⁡(t2){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}^{2}) CoT tokens: a Word RAM on a TM already incurs an 𝒪⁡(t2){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}^{2}) blowup,11 1 In general, each random-access step forces the TM to scan a tape region of length 𝒪⁡(t){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}) to reach the addressed cell. and the CoT spends one token per TM step. What is missing is a direct simulation at the Word RAM-instruction level—one that would let CoT transformers execute textbook algorithms at close to their textbook complexity.

We close this gap with direct Word RAM simulations for decoder-only CoT transformers in three settings. (i) First, finite-precision transformers of polylogarithmic width using rightmost-unique hard attention—an interpretable and pedagogical construction emitting 𝒪⁡(w2){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2})}} tokens per Word RAM instruction, hence 𝒪⁡(t​w2)=𝒪⁡(t​log2⁡(n+t)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\,{{w}}^{2})={{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\log^{2}({{n}}+{{t}})) tokens overall, with the per-instruction overhead dropping to 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} for multiplication-free instruction sets. This is essentially tight for discrete CoT: just as a Python program hard-coding a pp-bit integer must write Ω⁡(p){{\Omega}}(p) characters, any CoT transcript representing a w{{w}}-bit word must emit Ω⁡(w){{\Omega}}({{w}}) tokens from a fixed alphabet, giving an Ω⁡(t​w)=Ω⁡(t​log⁡(n+t)){{\Omega}}({{t}}\,{{w}})={{\Omega}}({{t}}\log({{n}}+{{t}})) lower bound. Our Word RAM simulation matches this bound up to one logarithmic factor in general and exactly when multiplication is excluded—already far below the Ω⁡(t2){{\Omega}}({{t}}^{2}) of TM-based CoT simulations. (ii) Second, fixed-width transformers with continuous CoT—which reasons with hidden vectors in place of discrete tokens. These models can invoke a TM oracle for each Word RAM instruction, generalizing the finite-precision setting. (iii) Third, hybrid models—transformers augmented with a linear RNN layer—which can implement the same simulation with explicit CoT. For an instruction set whose individual operations run in time κ⁡(w){\kappa}({{w}}) on a TM, the latter two constructions take 𝒪⁡(t​κ​(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\,{\kappa}({{w}})) CoT steps, generalizing the results to arbitrary instruction sets. This recovers the same poly-logarithmic overhead as the first setting: for the flat instruction sets we consider, κ⁡(w)=𝒪⁡(w){\kappa}({{w}})={{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}) when multiplication, division, and modulo are excluded and 𝒪⁡(w2){{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2}) otherwise, so 𝒪⁡(t​κ​(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\,{\kappa}({{w}})) is 𝒪⁡(t​log⁡(n+t)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\log({{n}}+{{t}})) or 𝒪⁡(t​log2⁡(n+t)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\log^{2}({{n}}+{{t}})) accordingly.

Contributions.

In summary, we prove that CoT transformers can directly simulate Word RAM algorithms with only poly-logarithmic overhead per instruction, matching an information-theoretic lower bound for discrete CoT up to a single logarithmic factor. Specifically, as summarized in Table 1:

  1. (i)

    Polylogarithmic-width transformers (Section 3). Fixed-precision transformers of log2⁡(n+t)\log^{2}({{n}}+{{t}}) width with rightmost-unique hard attention can simulate Word RAM programs. A Word RAM running t{{t}} steps with word size w=Θ⁡(log⁡(n+t)){{w}}={{\Theta}}(\log({{n}}+{{t}})) is simulated using 𝒪⁡(t⋅w2)=𝒪⁡(t​log2⁡(n+t)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\cdot{{w}}^{2})={{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\log^{2}({{n}}+{{t}})) tokens, dropping to 𝒪⁡(t⋅w)=𝒪⁡(t​log⁡(n+t)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\cdot{{w}})={{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\log({{n}}+{{t}})) for multiplication-free instruction sets. The latter matches the Ω⁡(t​w){{\Omega}}({{t}}\,{{w}}) lower bound for discrete CoT exactly, the former up to a single w{{w}} factor.

  2. (ii)

    Fixed-width transformers with continuous CoT (Section 5). A fixed-width, log-precision transformer augmented with continuous CoT—where each reasoning step is a real-valued vector rather than a discrete token—simulates any Word RAM program with 𝒪⁡(t⋅κ⁡(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\cdot{{\kappa}({{w}})}) decoding steps, where κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})} is the TM cost of executing one instruction.

  3. (iii)

    Hybrid transformer–RNN models (Section 6). A fixed-width transformer augmented with a single linear RNN layer simulates any Word RAM program at the same 𝒪⁡(t⋅κ⁡(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{t}}\cdot{{\kappa}({{w}})}) cost with explicit CoT, showing that recurrence is a natural and practical substitute for the width or continuity extensions of (i) and (ii).

2 Preliminaries

2.1 The Word RAM Computational Model

There are several different variants of Word RAMs in the literature with different instruction set details, ranging from C-like Word RAMs (Hagerup, 1998; Thorup, 1996; Morin, 2013) to the weaker multiplication-free basic instruction set of Brodnik et al. (1997). While classical literature has often explored various minimal, assembly-like instruction sets under which the model is Turing-complete, our goal here is different: we would like to argue that transformers and hybrid models, when equipped with CoT, can directly simulate programs even when they are written in a much higher-level language, such as “textbook algorithms” or simple Python programs, with only a log or log-square overhead. Note that this is a stronger claim than simulating a minimal instruction set with instructions like load, store, increment, etc., with a log or log-square overhead. Keeping this overhead small is important; after all, every Word RAM program can be converted to a Turing machine if one disregards the overhead (which, in general, would be quadratic), and then simulated using standard transformers with CoT via known constructions (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024).

Syntax. To this end, we define the following grammar for specifying Word RAM programs. Let n{{n}} be the input length, kk as the maximum number of variables (realized as registers) allowed in the Word RAM program, and c1, …\ldots, cm as the fixed constants (independent of n{{n}}) allowed in the program.

Line →\rightarrow Var = Expr | halt
Expr →\rightarrow Input | Const | Var | Expr Op Expr | UnOp Expr | Expr if Cond else Expr
Cond →\rightarrow Bool | Expr Comp Expr | Cond BoolOp Cond | ¬\neg Cond
Var →\rightarrow Reg | Mem | pc
Mem →\rightarrow mem[Expr]
Input →\rightarrow inp[Expr]
Reg →\rightarrow r1 | r2 | …\ldots | rk
Op →\rightarrow +|−|×|÷|mod|≪|≫|&|||⊕+|-|\times|\div|\bmod|\ll|\gg|\mathbin{\&}|\mathbin{|}|\oplus
BoolOp →\rightarrow ∧|∨\wedge|\vee
UnOp →\rightarrow ¬{\neg}
Comp →\rightarrow <|≤|=|≠|≥|><|\leq|=|\neq|\geq|>
Const →\rightarrow n | c1 | c2 | …\ldots | cm

The above grammar allows nesting of expressions (e.g., mem[mem[mem[7]]]) as well as composition of logical operators over conditionals via the Cond rule. We require that the nesting depth of every expression and condition be bounded by a constant independent of n{{n}}. This is what makes each line executable in 𝒪⁡(1){{\mathcal{O}}}(1) Word RAM steps. We also consider a simplified version of this grammar that doesn’t allow nesting. This is obtained by changing the grammar expansion rules for Expr and Cond to not be recursive, as follows:

FlatExpr →\rightarrow Input | Const | Var
Expr →\rightarrow FlatExpr | FlatExpr Op FlatExpr | UnOp FlatExpr | FlatExpr if Cond else FlatExpr
Cond →\rightarrow Bool | FlatExpr Comp FlatExpr

We call a Word RAM program flat if it uses only the flat grammar above. We further distinguish two flat instruction classes by which operators from Op appear: full-arithmetic flat programs may use any operator from Op, while simple-arithmetic flat programs restrict Op to {+,−,≪,≫,&,|,⊕}\{+,-,\ll,\gg,\mathbin{\&},\mathbin{|},\oplus\}, i.e., it excludes ×\times, ÷\div, mod\bmod.

Semantics. A specific Word RAM machine is specified by a finite-length program of the form above, with the standard semantics when executed on a string 𝒙∈Σ∗{{\bm{x}}}\in{{\Sigma}}^{*}. In more detail, the machine has three memory arrays: a read-only one inp that contains the input 𝒙{{\bm{x}}}, mem is a standard read-write tape initialized to all zeros, and out is an output tape that can only be written to, where written values are stored mod|Σ|\bmod\left\lvert{{\Sigma}}\right\rvert. The machine state also specifies the value of the program counter pc and finite registers r1,…,rk{\texttt{r1}},\ldots,{\texttt{rk}}, which all start as 0. When an instruction is run, pc is incremented, unless it is otherwise assigned by the instruction (e.g., pc=r2+1{\texttt{pc}}={\texttt{r2}}+1). The program runs until halt is executed, at which point the contents of out is deemed the output. When considering language recognition, we say that a Word RAM accepts a string iff out​[0]=1{\texttt{out}}[0]=1.

Without loss of generality, we can view the program counter pc and each register ri as stored in memory via pc≜mem​[0]{\texttt{pc}}\triangleq{\texttt{mem}}[0] and ri≜mem​[−i]{\texttt{ri}}\triangleq{\texttt{mem}}[-i], with mem being 1-indexed for standard memory.

2.2 Transformers and Related Models

Transformers. We defer a definition of the standard transformers model to Section A.1. The depth of our transformer will be fixed, i.e., 𝒪⁡(1){{\mathcal{O}}}(1), w.r.t. sequence length n{{n}} and CoT runtime t=𝒪⁡(nc)t={{\mathcal{O}}}({{n}}^{c}). Regarding precision and width of our transformers, we consider two possibilities motivated by a bifurcation in the transformer expressivity literature (Strobl et al., 2024; Svete et al., 2026):

  1. 1.

    Fixed precision and polylogarithmic, i.e., 𝒪⁡(logk⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}(\log^{k}{{n}}) width. Because width grows with n{{n}} and tt, this model is not fully uniform, meaning new parameters are introduced on longer inputs and CoTs. We use rightmost-unique hard attention transformers ( UHATs) (Strobl et al., 2024, cf.).

  2. 2.

    Logarithmic, i.e., 𝒪⁡(log⁡n){{\mathcal{O}}}(\log{{n}}), precision and fixed width. We further enforce in this model that the parameters are fully uniform. We use averaging hard attention (Strobl et al., 2024, cf.).

Linear RNNs and Hybrid Models. Next, we define linear RNN layers. There are many existing linear RNN architectures with complex parameterizations that all meet the following general form for different choices of AtA_{t}, btb_{t}, and ctc_{t} (Merrill et al., 2026): St+1=At​St+btS_{t+1}=A_{t}S_{t}+b_{t} and ht=ct⊤​Sth_{t}=c_{t}^{\top}S_{t} We will assume for simplicity that AtA_{t}, btb_{t}, and ctc_{t} are all parameterized as projections of the input vector to the RNN layer at step tt. RNNs can be fit into a transformer architecture by using the head input to compute At,btA_{t},b_{t}, and ctc_{t} and then defining hth_{t} as the head output. The sublayer output from a multihead RNN layer would then be passed through layer-norm in the standard way. A hybrid model is an architecture that mixes attention heads with linear RNN heads.

CoT. Finally, we say that a transformer TT computes a function ff within CoT budget t⁡(n)t({{n}}) if, after feeding 𝒙{{\bm{x}}} through TT and allowing at most t⁡(|w|)t(\left\lvert w\right\rvert) autoregressive steps sampled greedily (potentially terminating early), the generated tokens end with the suffix =f(w)${=}f(w){\$}, where ={=} is an output delimiter and ${\$} is the end-of-string symbol. Continuous CoT is defined analogously except that final logits of the transformer are passed as a “soft token” to the next step rather than a token decoded from them.

2.3 Layernorm Hash Representation

In the log-precision model, we will represent values vv using their layer-norm hash ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), which is a unit-norm vector in ℝ4{\mathbb{R}}^{4} defined as follows (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024):

ϕ⁡(v)≡ϕ⁡(v,1):=layernorm⁡(v,1,−v,−1)=(v,1,−v,−1)2​v2+2.\phi(v)\;\equiv\;\phi(v,1)\;:=\;{{\operatorname{layernorm}}}(v,1,-v,-1)\;=\;\frac{(v,1,-v,-1)}{\sqrt{2v^{2}+2}}. (1)

More generally, ϕ⁡(a,b)=layernorm⁡(a,b,−a,−b)\phi(a,b)={{\operatorname{layernorm}}}(a,b,-a,-b). This representation has several useful properties (similar to binary encodings) that we will leverage. The first property is useful for performing an equality check using inner product, as well as tie-breaking in order to simulate rightmost attention:

Proposition 1 (Equality Check and Mismatch Gap: Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024).

Let u,v∈{0,1,…,T}u,v\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}. Then ⟨ϕ⁡(u),ϕ⁡(v)⟩=1\langle\phi(u),\phi(v)\rangle=1 if and only if u=vu=v. Further, when u≠vu\neq v, ϕ(u),ϕ(v)⟩≤1−δT\phi(u),\phi(v)\rangle\leq 1-\delta_{T} where δT:=14​(T2+1)2\delta_{T}:=\frac{1}{4(T^{2}+1)^{2}}.

See proof in Section A.2 for completeness. ϕ\phi is scale invariant (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024): ϕ⁡(c​u,c​v)=ϕ⁡(u,v)=ϕ⁡(u/v,1)=ϕ⁡(u/v)\phi(cu,cv)=\phi(u,v)=\phi(u/v,1)=\phi(u/v). We can also “swap” the dimensions of ϕ\phi to invert a number: if ϕ⁡(v)=(s1,s2,−s1,−s2)\phi(v)=(s_{1},s_{2},-s_{1},-s_{2}), then ϕ⁡(1/v)=(s2,s1,−s2,−s1)\phi(1/v)=(s_{2},s_{1},-s_{2},-s_{1}). We introduce a new general affine update (proof in Section A.2), computable by a fixed-depth feedforward network as well as with an RNN:

Proposition 2 (Affine Update).

Fix constants a,b∈ℝa,b\in{\mathbb{R}}. Let ϕ⁡(v)=(s1,s2,−s1,−s2)\phi(v)=(s_{1},s_{2},-s_{1},-s_{2}). Then ϕ⁡(a​v+b)=layernorm⁡(a​s1+b​s2,s2,−(a​s1+b​s2),−s2)\phi(av+b)={{\operatorname{layernorm}}}(as_{1}+bs_{2},s_{2},-(as_{1}+bs_{2}),-s_{2}).

3 Simulating Word RAMs with Polylog-Width Transformers

We begin by showing how transformers with polylogarithmic width and fixed precision can simulate Word RAMs—a stepping stone towards more uniform transformer models, which do not require new parameters as the input length grows. Thus, we use the construction in this section to cleanly outline the simulation; the main ideas will re-appear in the subsequent sections.

The transformer model. We use a log2\log^{2}-width finite-precision transformer model; see Remark 2 for a discussion of why log2\log^{2} width is needed. The constructions build on the log-width machinery formalized by existing work (Li et al., 2024; Svete et al., 2025; Svete and Sabharwal, 2026).22 2 In particular, we use 𝖫\mathsf{L}-uniform transformers (London and Kanade, 2025), (Barcelo et al., 2026, §4.4) with positional encodings that only contain the binary representation of the position. This prevents the PEs from encoding too much information and relies on the transformer abilities to simulate the Word RAM programs. This allows us to reuse existing gadgets in our constructions.

Representation of values. In the polylogarithmic-width setting, word-sized integers are stored in the residual stream as binary vectors denoting their binary expansions: for a value v∈{0,1}wv\in\{0,1\}^{{w}}, the representation repr⁡(v)=defbits⁡(v)∈{0,1}w{{\operatorname{repr}}}(v)\mathrel{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\textnormal{\tiny def}}}{{=}}}{{\operatorname{bits}}}(v)\in\{0,1\}^{{w}} is placed directly as a vector in the residual stream. This gives two primitives: (i) equality checkingvia inner products (repr⁡(i)⊤​repr⁡(j)=w{{\operatorname{repr}}}(i)^{\top}{{\operatorname{repr}}}(j)={{w}} iff i=ji=j, and strictly less otherwise), and (ii) bit extractionvia repr⁡(v)⊤​𝒆t=bt{{{\operatorname{repr}}}(v)^{\top}{{{\bm{e}}}}_{t}}=b_{t} for the t​tht\textsuperscript{th} standard basis vector 𝒆t{{{\bm{e}}}}_{t}. These two primitives are the key gadgets exploited throughout this section; the subsequent sections will define different representations to maintain fixed width.

Theorem 1 formalizes Word RAM simulation by log2\log^{2}-width transformers; see Appendix C for the full proof.

Theorem 1 (Simulation of Word RAMs by log2\log^{2}-Width Transformers).

Let MM be a flat Word RAM program with word size w{{w}}. Then there exists a rightmost UHAT  TT with finite precision, 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} heads each of width 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}}, and total model dimension 𝒪⁡(w2)=𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n+t)){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2})}}={{{{\mathcal{O}}}(\log^{2}({{n}}+t))}}, such that, for any t≥nt\geq{{n}}, TT can simulate tt steps of MM with t⋅𝒪⁡(w2)t\cdot{{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2})}} CoT steps. Further, if MM does not use ×\times, ÷\div, or mod\bmod, TT can simulate tt steps of MM with t⋅𝒪⁡(w)t\cdot{{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} CoT steps.

Proof sketch.

Following the Word RAM definition (Section 2.1), the Word RAM state—program counter, registers, and memory—is folded into a single random-access memory mem. The construction logs every memory write to the CoT transcript as a memory block of the form mem​#​bits⁡(a)​#​bits​(v){\texttt{{\color[rgb]{0.6406,0.0273,0.4531}mem}}}\,{\texttt{\#}}\,{{\operatorname{bits}}}(a)\,{\texttt{\#}}\,{{\operatorname{bits}}}(v) (Figure 1). The central operation is the memory read (Lemma 12): given a query address bits⁡(a){{\operatorname{bits}}}(a) in the residual stream, recover the value of the rightmost mem block whose address field encodes aa (i.e., the most recent write to mem​[a]{\texttt{mem}}[a]). This uses two attention steps: the first selects the rightmost matching address position; the second retrieves the value field at the known offset.

Each CoT step runs four constant-depth layer blocks (cf. Figure 4 and Appendix C): (i) Load pc:an indexed read with the constant query 00 recovers bits⁡(mem​[0]){{\operatorname{bits}}}({\texttt{mem}}[0]) in two attention layers (Proposition 3); (ii) Load Instruction and Operands:the active line of the program is identified from bits⁡(mem​[0]){{\operatorname{bits}}}({\texttt{mem}}[0]) by an MLP that issues parallel reads of every compile-time address listed in the instruction’s operand descriptor (registers), and a second round of reads resolves any runtime addresses (mem​[a]{\texttt{mem}}[a] or inp​[a]{\texttt{inp}}[a]) whose index aa is now in the residual stream (Proposition 4); (iii) Execute:a single MLP computes the w{{w}}-bit destination value(s) and the next pc from the operands now in the residual stream (Proposition 5); (iv) Store:an attention layer computes the within-step offset δ\delta from the rightmost &, and the appropriate δth\delta^{\text{th}} token (a mem, a #, an address bit, a value bit, or &) is emitted as the output token (Proposition 6).

For simple instructions, Blocks (i)–(iii) produce identical outputs at every token within the same step, so only δ\delta advances in Block (iv), emitting one token at a time over 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} total positions. Deserialization uses w{{w}} dedicated attention heads (one per bit), each of width w{{w}}, giving the 𝒪⁡(w2)=𝒪⁡(log2⁡(n+t)){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2})}}={{{{\mathcal{O}}}(\log^{2}({{n}}+t))}} model dimension. In contrast to simple instructions, multiplication, division, and modulo cannot be computed in a single transformer step and are compiled into 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} flat micro-steps that share state through program-private memory cells. Each micro-step costs 𝒪⁡(w){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}})}} tokens, for 𝒪⁡(w2){{{{\mathcal{O}}}({{w}}^{2})}} total; every micro-step uses the same four-block pipeline (Proposition 7). ∎

Corollary 1.

Let MM and TT be as in Theorem 1. We have the following:

  1. (i)

    TT can simulate tt steps of MM with full-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log2​t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log^{2}t) steps.

  2. (ii)

    TT can simulate tt steps of MM with simple-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log⁡t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log t) steps.

Remark 1 (Bit extraction as a dot product).

Reading from and writing into the CoT transcript both require bit extraction: computing BIT⁡(v,t){{\operatorname{BIT}}}(v,t), the t​tht\textsuperscript{th} bit of vv. In the log2\log^{2}-width setting this is trivial: since bits⁡(v)∈{0,1}w{{\operatorname{bits}}}(v)\in\{0,1\}^{{w}} is stored as a coordinate vector in the residual stream, extracting btb_{t} reduces to the dot product bits⁡(v)⊤​𝒆t=bt{{{\operatorname{bits}}}(v)^{\top}{{{\bm{e}}}}_{t}}=b_{t} with the t​tht\textsuperscript{th} standard basis vector 𝒆t{{{\bm{e}}}}_{t}. In the fixed-width constructions later, bits⁡(v){{\operatorname{bits}}}(v) is no longer directly available as a coordinate vector, so bit extraction becomes substantially more involved and is one of the primary sources of complexity in those proofs.

These results provide a general framework for how CoT can simulate Word RAM programs. However, the log2\log^{2}-width construction is non-uniform: the model grows with n{{n}}, so new parameters—untrained on shorter inputs—must be invoked as the inputs grow longer. The construction also requires rightmost UHAT; we show in Remark 3 that weaker attention models cannot implement the indexed-read step. The fixed-width constructions in the following sections avoid the non-uniformity and reliance on rightmost UHATs at the cost of more complex reading and writing mechanisms.

4 Towards a Uniform Fixed-Width Construction: Bottlenecks and Plan

In Section 3, storing bits⁡(v){{\operatorname{bits}}}(v) in the residual stream gives three things for free: (i) equality checking via inner products, (ii) bit extraction via bits⁡(v)⊤​𝒆t=bt{{{\operatorname{bits}}}(v)^{\top}{{{\bm{e}}}}_{t}}=b_{t}, and (iii) a clean serialization/deserialization mechanism. Moving to fixed width forces us to abandon the bits{{\operatorname{bits}}} representation, and each of these primitives must be rebuilt from scratch. We describe the resulting challenges below.

Bottleneck: Reading and writing values. The deepest challenge in moving to fixed width is that we must adopt a different representation of numbers in the residual stream. For fixed-width constructions, any such representation repr{{\operatorname{repr}}} of values must satisfy two properties simultaneously:

  1. (a)

    Equality gap: repr⁡(i)⊤​repr⁡(j)=1{{\operatorname{repr}}}(i)^{\top}{{\operatorname{repr}}}(j)=1 if i=ji=j, and repr⁡(i)⊤​repr⁡(j)<1−ϵ{{\operatorname{repr}}}(i)^{\top}{{\operatorname{repr}}}(j)<1-\epsilon otherwise.

  2. (b)

    Read/write: We can serialize repr⁡(v){{\operatorname{repr}}}(v) to a binary CoT encoding and recover repr⁡(v){{\operatorname{repr}}}(v) from it.

The first property is needed for the indexed-read attention mechanism; the second is needed both (a) to pass pointers computed at a higher layer back to lower layers in future steps, and (b) to hand binary-encoded operands to the TM oracle for complex arithmetic. Past work has established the layer-norm hash ϕ⁡(i)\phi(i) as a fixed-width representation satisfying the equality-gap property (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024), but reading and writing via ϕ\phi presents a challenge.

Writing is hard because it requires computing BIT⁡(v,j){{\operatorname{BIT}}}(v,j) from ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v)---mapping a hash representation back to individual bits.33 3 BIT⁡(v,j){{\operatorname{BIT}}}(v,j) plays a central role in descriptive complexity theory and the analysis of transformer expressivity. One approach is to compute ϕ⁡(vmod2)\phi(v\bmod 2) and ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor) iteratively. When v≤tv\leq t, Merrill and Sabharwal (2025) give a construction for computing ϕ⁡(vmod2)\phi(v\bmod 2) and ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor) from ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v); for larger values this is open (note that Proposition 2 allows easily computing ϕ⁡(v/2)\phi(v/2), but not ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)). To resolve the write challenge, we adopt a normal form for Word RAMs that enforces v≤tv\leq t at every step, developed in Section 4.1, allowing us to compute the least significant bit of vv as well as ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor). The remaining bits of vv can be obtained by iterating the process, which requires repeatedly conditioning on ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor), ϕ⁡(⌊v/4⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/4\rfloor), etc. We show this can be achieved via either of two minimal architectural extensions: continuous CoT (Section 5, Lemma 5) or hybrid transformer–RNN models (Section 6, Lemma 8).44 4 This iterative computation can also be performed by a logarithmic-depth transformer; we do not explore this here.

Reading is hard for a complementary reason: while ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) can be reconstructed from a binary CoT encoding via iterative bit-shifting within the ϕ\phi representation, this is not known to be achievable by a plain transformer. We show that this too becomes feasible with either of two minimal architectural extensions: continuous CoT (Section 5, Lemma 7) and hybrid transformer–RNN models (Section 6, Lemma 9).4

4.1 Writing Solution: Equivalent RAMs with Bounded Word Values

We define a cc-dimensional Word RAM as a Word RAM where the tape is replaced by a cc-dimensional array of cc-dimensional tuples. The following lemma shows that such Word RAMs are as powerful as standard Word RAMs, up to a constant factor in runtime (see Appendix B for a proof):

Lemma 1.

Let MM be a 1-dimensional Word RAM with word size w=c​log⁡(n+t)w=c\log(n+t) for some c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N}. Then there exists a cc-dimensional restricted Word RAM M′M^{\prime} with word size w′=log⁡(n+t)w^{\prime}=\log(n+t) and the same instruction set as MM that simulates tt steps of MM using 𝒪⁡(t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t) steps.

This shows that we can reduce any MM using word size w=c​log⁡(n+t)w=c\log(n+t) to M′M^{\prime} using word size w=log⁡(n+t)w=\log(n+t). Now, define a Word RAM as restricted if, for any step ii, any value vv represented in any register satisfies v≤iv\leq i. Any Word RAM MM can be converted to be restricted by making it do nothing for the first vv steps, and then simulating the ii-th step of MM at step v+iv+i:

Lemma 2.

Let MM be any cc-dimensional Word RAM where all values are at most v⁡(n)v(n) on inputs of size nn. Then there exists M′M^{\prime} that simulates tt steps of MM using v⁡(n)+tv(n)+t steps such that, at each step ii, all values in M′M^{\prime} are at most ii.

We can first invoke Lemma 1 and then apply Lemma 2 with v⁡(n)=n+tv(n)=n+t to obtain the following:

Theorem 2 (Restricted Word RAM Equivalence).

A standard Word RAM running in time t⁡(n)t(n) on inputs of size nn can be simulated by a restricted cc-dimensional Word RAM in time 𝒪⁡(n+t⁡(n)){{\mathcal{O}}}(n+t(n)).

This will be useful because simulating restricted Word RAMs with transformer-like models will be easier than simulating unrestricted ones. Specifically, the property v≤iv\leq i will be useful for writing numbers in binary as it allows us to divide numbers using attention via the following special case of the “division lemma” of Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) where the divisor is 22 (see Appendix B for a proof):

Lemma 3 (Simplified Division Lemma).

There exists a transformer block that, for any ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) present in the residual stream at position tt for v≤tv\leq t, adds ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\left\lfloor v/2\right\rfloor) and ϕ⁡(vmod2)\phi(v\bmod 2) to the residual stream.

This will be useful for writing numbers ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) onto the CoT in binary because it allows computing the least significant bit via ϕ⁡(vmod2)\phi(v\bmod 2), or ϕ⁡(vmod2i)\phi(v\bmod 2^{i}), which can be useful for recovering other bits.

5 Simulating Word RAMs with Continuous CoT

The bounded-value normal form from Section 4.1 ensures a crucial bit-extraction precondition: during execution, every word vv at RAM step ss satisfies v≤sv\leq s. Since each simulated step produces at least one transcript symbol, this implies v≤τv\leq\tau whenever the simulator begins emitting a bit-string segment at transcript position τ\tau. Thus, whenever we need to stream a word as bits we may apply the simplified division primitive (Lemma 3) to compute ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor) and ϕ⁡(vmod2)\phi(v\bmod 2) (the first bit) from ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), and then repeat the process for the next bit by conditioning the computation on ϕ⁡(⌊v/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor), and so on.

The remaining obstacle is persistence: after streaming ww discrete bits, later computation must still have access to a constant-dimensional word code that supports exact-match attention (for RAM addressing) and can be carried forward across time.

We show that continuous CoT can be used to achieve both conditioning and persistence.

Continuous CoT and soft tokens. In the continuous-CoT model, each decoding step emits both (i) a discrete token from a fixed alphabet and (ii) a constant-dimensional soft token pi∈ℝdsp_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d_{s}}. The next decoding step receives the entire prefix, including the past soft tokens, so pip_{i} can be attended to by future layers. In particular, a constant-depth transformer block can copy designated coordinates of the most recent soft token forward (e.g. via a fixed-offset retrieval head), so the soft token acts as a small persistent register bank threaded through the transcript.

Theorem 3 (Simulating Word RAMs with CCoT).

Let MM be a dd-dimensional-array Word RAM with word size w=log⁡(n+t)+𝒪⁡(1)w=\log(n+t)+{{\mathcal{O}}}(1) and per-instruction bit-serial cost bound κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})}.55 5 Here κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})} counts decoding steps of a fixed-alphabet bit-serial implementation of a RAM instruction on ww-bit operands, including the unavoidable Ω⁡(w)\Omega(w) serialization of any fresh ww-bit output word over a fixed alphabet. Then there exists a log-precision, finite-width continuous CoT transformer TT such that, for any t≥nt\geq n, tt steps of MM can be simulated by TT using 𝒪⁡(t​κ​(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\,{{\kappa}({{w}})}) decoding steps.

Proof overview.

We prove Theorem 3 by induction on the simulated RAM step ss. The simulator maintains an append-only transcript whose soft token stores the pair (ϕ⁡(a),ϕ⁡(v))(\phi(a),\phi(v)) for the written address/value mem​[a]←v{\texttt{mem}}[a]\leftarrow v (absorbing pc and registers into mem; see Section 2.1). Checkpoint and store-summary positions are marked by constant discrete tags so attention can restrict to the relevant subset. If no store-summary exists for an address aa, the value at mem​[a]{\texttt{mem}}[a] is interpreted as 00. A useful property of continuous CoT is that we can always make the latest checkpoint available “from layer 0” at future positions: a constant-depth carry block can attend to the rightmost checkpoint tag and copy its soft-token coordinates into designated coordinates of the current residual stream.

One simulated RAM step. Assume the invariant holds at the end of RAM step ss. To simulate step s+1s{+}1, we perform the following conceptual phases (some happen within a single decoding step, others take many decoding steps), illustrated in Figure 2:

  1. (1)

    Load pc. Attend to the rightmost checkpoint and copy ϕ⁡(PC(s))\phi({{\operatorname{PC}}}^{(s)}) (and the register codes) into the current residual stream. Use PC(s){{\operatorname{PC}}}^{(s)} to select which instruction subroutine/oracle to run.

  2. (2)

    Load operand values. For each register/constant operand, read ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) directly from the copied checkpoint state. For each memory operand mem​[a]{\texttt{mem}}[a], form ϕ⁡(a)\phi(a) and dereference the most recent matching store-summary to recover the operand in coded form ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) (Lemma 4).

  3. (3)

    Serialize inputs (write a binary tape). For each coded input word needed by the instruction oracle, emit its ww bits onto the discrete transcript using Lemma 5. This creates a delimited work-tape suffix for the instruction oracle.

  4. (4)

    Instruction execution (TM oracle). Activate the instruction-specific TM-oracle subroutine, which operates only on the work-tape suffix and runs for 𝒪⁡(κ⁡(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{\kappa}({{w}})}) decoding steps, emitting the output words as bit streams (Lemma 6).

  5. (5)

    Deserialize outputs. Convert each output bit stream into its coded form ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) for future addressing and equality tests, using Lemma 7.

  6. (6)

    Store updates (re-establish the invariant). Emit a new checkpoint token whose soft token stores the updated state ϕ⁡(PC(s+1)),ϕ⁡(r1(s+1)),…,ϕ⁡(rρ(s+1))\phi({{\operatorname{PC}}}^{(s+1)}),\phi(r_{1}^{(s+1)}),\ldots,\phi(r_{{{\rho}}}^{(s+1)}). If the instruction writes mem​[a]←v{\texttt{mem}}[a]\leftarrow v, also emit a store-summary token storing (ϕ⁡(a),ϕ⁡(v))(\phi(a),\phi(v)). By construction, this new checkpoint (and store-summary, if present) is the rightmost such entry, so it will be used at the next step.

Correctness follows from induction on ss: step (5) appends the new rightmost checkpoint encoding the updated registers/PC, and appends the new rightmost store-summary for any updated address. The total number of decoding steps spent in phases (2)–(4) is 𝒪⁡(w+κ⁡(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}(w+{{\kappa}({{w}})}) per RAM instruction, yielding 𝒪⁡(t​κ​(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\,{{\kappa}({{w}})}) steps overall. The following lemmas implement each step (proofs in Appendix D).

Lemma 4 (Steps 1–2: loading values).

Suppose the transcript contains store-summary positions, each tagged and whose soft token stores a pair (ϕ⁡(aj),ϕ⁡(vj))(\phi(a_{j}),\phi(v_{j})). Let τ\tau be a transcript position at which a query address aa is available as ϕ⁡(a)\phi(a) in the residual stream, and suppose a≤τa\leq\tau. Then a log-precision, finite-width continuous-CoT transformer can retrieve ϕ⁡(vj∗)\phi(v_{j^{*}}), where j∗j^{*} is the largest index with aj∗=aa_{j^{*}}=a. If no such j∗j^{*} exists, it retrieves ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0).

Lemma 5 (Step 3: serialization).

Let τ\tau be a transcript position at which a value vv is available as ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the residual stream, and suppose v≤τv\leq\tau. Then a log-precision, finite-width continuous-CoT transformer can emit the w{{w}} bits of vv over the next w{{w}} decoding steps, ordered from least to most significant, while keeping ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) available in designated coordinates of the soft token throughout.

Lemma 6 (Step 4: instruction execution).

Fix any RAM instruction II on w{{w}}-bit operands whose bit-serial implementation runs in κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})} decoding steps. There exists a log-precision, finite-width continuous-CoT transformer subnetwork that, once activated, simulates this bit-serial computation for 𝒪⁡(κ⁡(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}({{\kappa}({{w}})}) decoding steps and emits the output bit streams of II onto the transcript. Moreover, the subnetwork can be made to ignore the rest of the transcript by delimiting a work-tape suffix (with a start marker) and restricting all attention inside the subroutine to positions in that suffix.

Lemma 7 (Step 5: deserialization).

There exists a log-precision, finite-width continuous-CoT transformer that, on bit sequence b0,…,bw−1b_{0},\ldots,b_{{{w}}-1} followed by w{{w}} arbitrary tokens, computes ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the residual stream at the last step, where v=∑k=0w−1bk​2kv=\sum_{k=0}^{{{w}}-1}b_{k}2^{k} is the LSB evaluation of bb.

Step 6: storing new values. We emit a soft token encoding the target position to write to (from load step) as kk and the output value (from deserialize) as vv. This completes the store step, satisfying our inductive invariant for step s+1s+1, which completes the proof. ∎

We have the following consequences of Theorem 3, depending on the complexity of the instruction set:

Corollary 2 (Simulating Word RAMs with CCoT).

Let MM and TT be as in Theorem 3. Depending on the complexity of the instruction set κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})} of MM, the following hold:

  1. (i)

    TT can simulate tt steps of MM with arbitrary poly​(w)\textrm{poly}({{w}})-time instructions using 𝒪~​(t){{\tilde{\mathcal{O}}}}(t) steps.

  2. (ii)

    TT can simulate tt steps of MM with full-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log2​t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log^{2}t) steps.

  3. (iii)

    TT can simulate tt steps of MM with simple-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log⁡t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log t) steps.

6 Simulating Word RAMs with Hybrid Models

Finally, we show that, similarly to using CCoT, leveraging hybrid models that mix transformer and linear RNN components allow simulating a Word RAM:

Theorem 4 (Simulating Word RAMs with Hybrid Models).

Let MM be a cc-dimensional-array Word RAM with word size w=log⁡(n+t)+𝒪⁡(1)w=\log(n+t)+{{\mathcal{O}}}(1) and maximum instruction cost κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})}. Then there exists a log-precision, fixed-width hybrid model HH with a single RNN layer at the bottom such that, for any t≥nt\geq n, tt steps of MM can be simulated by HH using 𝒪⁡(t​κ​(w)){{\mathcal{O}}}(t{{\kappa}({{w}})}) steps.

Let v=∑k=0w−1bk​2kv=\sum_{k=0}^{w-1}b_{k}2^{k}. The proof of this theorem is structurally identical to that of Theorem 3 for transformers with continuous CoT, except for the way values vv, represented as ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the residual stream, are serialized as bits b0,b1,…,bw−1b_{0},b_{1},\ldots,b_{w-1} via CoT, and the way bits b0,b1,…,bw−1b_{0},b_{1},\ldots,b_{w-1} in the input layer are deserialized as ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the residual stream. Since we no longer have access to soft tokens in the CoT output, we cannot simply emit intermediate ϕ\phi representations as part of the CoT to condition upon in the next step. However, we can use a similar ability afforded by RNNs, which naturally allow conditioning on values available in the residual stream at the immediately previous position.

The only other difference is in the store step, where the continuous CoT captures operations of the form mem​[a]←v{\texttt{mem}}[a]\leftarrow v by emitting a store-summary soft token storing (ϕ⁡(a),ϕ⁡(v))(\phi(a),\phi(v)). Instead, we now serialize aa and vv using ww bits each via the (updated) serialization lemma below, and use the (updated) deserialization lemma on these bits to obtain ϕ⁡(a)\phi(a) and ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the layer 11 residual stream after ww additional dummy tokens.

All other steps in the construction for Theorem 3 remain unchanged. In the remainder of this section, we thus focus on deriving counterparts of Lemmas 5 and 7 for hybrid architectures. The serialization construction is essentially the same as in the proof of Lemma 5, except that without continuous CoT, we cannot emit ϕ⁡(vk+1)\phi(v_{k+1}), defined as ϕ⁡(⌊vk/2⌋)\phi(\lfloor v_{k}/2\rfloor), at position τ+k+1\tau+k+1 and read it back in at the following position. Instead, we emit bkb_{k}, computed via Lemma 3. We then compute ϕ⁡(⌊vk/2⌋)\phi(\left\lfloor v_{k}/2\right\rfloor) from ϕ⁡(vk)\phi(v_{k}) and bkb_{k} via its equivalent form ϕ⁡(12​(vk−bk))\phi(\frac{1}{2}(v_{k}-b_{k})) by leveraging Proposition 2 to turn it into a linear transformation that an RNN head can perform. This gives the following result (proof in Appendix E):

Lemma 8 (Serialization).

Let τ\tau be a transcript position at which a value vv is available as ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v) in the residual stream, and suppose v≤τv\leq\tau. Then a log-precision, finite-width hybrid model can emit the ww bits of vv over the next ww decoding steps, ordered from least to most significant.

For deserialization, we use the same recursive computation as in the corresponding lemma for continuous CoT (Lemma 7), except now the computation is within the hidden state of the linear RNN rather than via soft tokens. This gives the following result (proof in Appendix E):

Lemma 9 (Deserialization).

There exists a log-precision, finite-width hybrid model that, on any bit sequence b0,…,bw−1b_{0},\ldots,b_{w-1} followed by ww arbitrary tokens, computes ϕ⁡(v)\phi(v), where v=∑k=0w−1bk​2kv=\sum_{k=0}^{w-1}b_{k}2^{k} is the LSB evaluation of bb, in the residual stream at depth 11 at the last token.

Analogously to Corollary 2 for the CCoT simulation, we have the following notable cases:

Corollary 3 (Simulating Word RAM with Hybrid Models).

Let MM and HH be as in Theorem 4. Depending on the complexity of the instruction set κ⁡(w){{\kappa}({{w}})} of MM, the following hold:

  1. (i)

    HH can simulate tt steps of MM with arbitrary poly​(w)\textrm{poly}({{w}})-time instructions using 𝒪~​(t){{\tilde{\mathcal{O}}}}(t) steps.

  2. (ii)

    HH can simulate tt steps of MM with full-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log2​t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log^{2}t) steps.

  3. (iii)

    HH can simulate tt steps of MM with simple-arithmetic flat instructions using 𝒪⁡(t​log⁡t){{\mathcal{O}}}(t\log t) steps.

7 Conclusion

We show that poly-logarithmic-width transformers can simulate a Word RAM; while it is unclear whether fixed-width transformers can also do so, we show that two minimal extensions to fixed-width transformers (continuous CoT transformers and hybrid models) both can. Our results show that CoT—at least for certain architectures—allows simulating algorithms with their general textbook runtimes up to a polylogarithmic factor, removing the quadratic overhead that would be incurred by going through previously established Turing completeness results (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). Since certain realistic extensions (continuous CoT or RNN layers) to transformers are crucial for the fixed-width constructions, it is an interesting open question to what degree these extensions are necessary for efficient Word RAM simulation. It would also be interesting to study to what degree these extensions benefit algorithmic reasoning in transformer models in practice.

Appendix A Details on the Preliminaries

A.1 The Transformer Model

This appendix restates the decoder-only transformer model used in Merrill and Sabharwal [2024], which itself builds on the component-level formalization of Merrill and Sabharwal [2023a]. Let Σ{{\Sigma}} be the fixed token alphabet. Let 𝔻p\mathbb{D}_{p} be the datatype of pp-bit floating-point numbers with truncated arithmetic as in Merrill and Sabharwal [2023b].

Definition 1 (Decoder-only transformer).

A pp-precision decoder-only transformer with hh heads, dd layers, model dimension mm, and feedforward width uu consists of: (i) an embedding map e:Σ×𝕟→𝔻pme:{{\Sigma}}\times\mathbb{{{n}}}\to\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}; (ii) for each layer ℓ\ell and head kk, a similarity map skℓ:𝔻pm×𝔻pm→𝔻ps_{k}^{\ell}:\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}\times\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}\to\mathbb{D}_{p} and a value map vkℓ:𝔻pm→𝔻pm/hv_{k}^{\ell}:\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}\to\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m/h}; (iii) for each layer ℓ\ell, an activation map fℓ:(𝔻pm/h)h×𝔻pm→𝔻pmf^{\ell}:(\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m/h})^{h}\times\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}\to\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}; (iv) an output map γ:𝔻pm→Σ′\gamma:\mathbb{D}_{p}^{m}\to{{\Sigma}}^{\prime}.

Definition 2 (One strict-causal decoding step).

For a prefix z=z1⋯znz=z_{1}\cdots z_{n}, set 𝐡i0=e⁡(zi,i)\mathbf{h}_{i}^{0}=e(z_{i},i). For each layer ℓ\ell and head kk, define

𝐚i,kℓ=∑j<iskℓ​(𝐡iℓ−1,𝐡jℓ−1)Zi,kℓ​vkℓ​(𝐡jℓ−1),Zi,kℓ=∑j<iskℓ​(𝐡iℓ−1,𝐡jℓ−1).\mathbf{a}_{i,k}^{\ell}=\sum_{j<i}\frac{s_{k}^{\ell}(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\ell-1},\mathbf{h}_{j}^{\ell-1})}{Z_{i,k}^{\ell}}\,v_{k}^{\ell}(\mathbf{h}_{j}^{\ell-1}),\qquad Z_{i,k}^{\ell}=\sum_{j<i}s_{k}^{\ell}(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\ell-1},\mathbf{h}_{j}^{\ell-1}).

Then

𝐡iℓ=fℓ​(𝐚i,1ℓ,…,𝐚i,hℓ,𝐡iℓ−1),g⁡(z)=γ⁡(𝐡nd).\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\ell}=f^{\ell}(\mathbf{a}_{i,1}^{\ell},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{i,h}^{\ell},\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\ell-1}),\qquad g(z)=\gamma(\mathbf{h}_{n}^{d}).
Definition 3 (Projected pre-norm).

For a residual vector 𝐡\mathbf{h} and a linear map 𝐌\mathbf{M}, projected pre-norm applies layer norm to 𝐌𝐡\mathbf{M}\mathbf{h}:

PLN⁡(𝐡,𝐌)=LN⁡(𝐌𝐡).{{\operatorname{PLN}}}(\mathbf{h};\mathbf{M})={{\operatorname{LN}}}(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{h}).

We note that now-standard peri-norm [Kim et al., 2025] or reordered norm [Olmo, 2026], which did not exist at the time of Merrill and Sabharwal [2024], allows implementing projected pre-norm constructions with no extra projection. With reordered norm, we can simply always write normalized values at the layer output and then apply a projection to select those values when needed. With peri-norm, the same idea works: all writes to the residual stream are normalized, so when we read a normalized vector at the next sublayer input, the number of writes gets normalized away with no distortions.

As in Merrill and Sabharwal [2024], the lower-bound construction does not depend on any special positional encoding. We assume standard causal masking rather than strict causal masking.

We will show how to simulate MM with M′M^{\prime}. The following invariant will be helpful: MM has size w=c​w′w=cw^{\prime}, so any value xx can represented with cc values x1′,…,xc′x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{c}, each of word size w′w^{\prime}.

For any instruction in MM that retrieves the value at xx and stores it into yy, we will instead have cc instructions that retrieve the value at each xi′x^{\prime}_{i} and store it into yi′y^{\prime}_{i} for 1≤i≤c1\leq i\leq c. Similarly, whenever we write the value at yy into xx, we will have cc instructions that write value yi′y^{\prime}_{i} into xi′x^{\prime}_{i}. Thus, each read or write instruction in MM can be simulated by cc instructions in M′M^{\prime}.

It remains to be shown that arithmetic instructions in MM can also be simulated in M′M^{\prime}:

    Adding xx and yy in MM can be implemented in M′M^{\prime} by starting with κ1=0\kappa_{1}=0 and adding blocks xi′+yi′+κix^{\prime}_{i}+y^{\prime}_{i}+\kappa_{i} iteratively for i=1,2,…,ci=1,2,\ldots,c, with κi+1=𝟙[x′+y′≥2w]\kappa_{i+1}={\mathbbm{1}[x^{\prime}+y^{\prime}\geq 2^{w}]} being the carry bit for the subsequent step.   • •

    Subtracting mirrors addition, with the borrow bit βi+1=𝟙[x′+βi<y′]\beta_{i+1}={\mathbbm{1}[x^{\prime}+\beta_{i}<y^{\prime}]}. (If the final borrow bit βc+1=1\beta_{c+1}=1, the result is negative.)

Then position tt attends back to find the closest multiple of mm via rightmost hard attention to compute the mod and div values.

In our special use case, we can simplify this process as follows: each position j<tj<t computes a key kj=ϕ⁡(2​j)k_{j}=\phi(2j) and value ϕ⁡(j)\phi(j). Position tt uses query qt=ϕ⁡(v−1)q_{t}=\phi(v-1), which can be computed via Proposition 2. It can be verified that the closest matching key is k⌈(v−1)/2⌉k_{\left\lceil(v-1)/2\right\rceil},77 7 Suppose vv is odd, i.e., v=2​j∗+1v=2j^{*}+1 for some integer j∗j^{*}.
